Dear Irfan,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Here's the truth. At Onam I told Achan I'm not sure I want to take over the ayurvedic pharmacy. I didn't say no. I said I want one year at design school first, to see what's mine and what I just grew up inside. Achan went quiet. Then Valiyamma said, loud enough for the whole table, 'After everything they gave you, this is how you repay them? Ungrateful.' Nobody disagreed. I've been in my hostel room for three days since. I feel guilty every time I open my sketchbook, like I'm stealing from them. And I feel so alone, because I can't say any of this at home. I love that shop. I'm only asking a question. Is that so wrong?
Write back soon,
Jeevan

qa.a: Jeevan feels guilty, as if stealing from the family, and lonely because none of it can be said at home.

qa.a: Irfan could reassure Jeevan that asking questions isn't betrayal and suggest a calm talk with Achan about the one-year plan.

qa.a: Achan may be hurt or worried about the pharmacy's future, which could explain the silence, even without anger.

grounding: A young adult who questions taking over the family business is called ungrateful and feels guilty and alone while asking what is truly theirs.

passage: Vinita, you asked on our walk why I've been so quiet since Diwali. Okay. I'm Sharmila, I'm twenty, and I've gone to satsang with my family every Sunday of my life. This year I started reading, asking questions, visiting other places of worship with friends, just to understand. I didn't stop believing. I just wanted to know which parts were mine. At the Diwali puja my Masi said, in front of everyone, 'Sharmila has lost her way. College has spoiled her.' Mummy didn't defend me. She just looked sad. I felt like a traitor for even having questions, and after that I sat alone in the car during the aarti. The loneliest part is that I still love the bhajans. I just want to love them because I chose to, not because I was born into them.

'Your grandfather built that business with his own hands, and you want to go and play schoolmaster? You're lost.' Nobody spoke. Vaibhav's ears burned all afternoon.
Wednesday: he sat in the college library with two forms in front of him, the internship and the teaching fellowship, and couldn't sign either. Every time he picked up the teaching one, he felt ungrateful, and very alone.
The following Sunday: his sister Ira slipped into his room. 'You're not lost. You're asking. That's different.' She had printed the fellowship's dates: six weeks, done by July. 'Do this, then three weeks at the office. Then you'll actually know.' Vaibhav laughed for the first time in a week.

qa.a: 'You're lost.'

qa.a: Vaibhav felt guilty and very alone, unable to sign either form because choosing teaching felt ungrateful.

qa.a: Ira sees it as honest asking, not being lost, and wants to help her brother find out what is really his.

Saturday.
Two years into being a CA and today I finally admitted it: I became one because Papa and Vandana Didi did, and I never once asked if I wanted to. I don't hate the numbers. I actually like the puzzle of an audit. What I hate is that I never chose it. So I'm not quitting, not dramatically anyway. I've signed up for the Saturday photography course, and I told my firm I'll take the four-day week they offered last year. Tonight I told Didi. I was ready for a fight. I said, 'You and Papa gave me a good path. I'm keeping the parts I like, and trying something that's mine.' She was quiet, then asked what camera I wanted. I nearly cried into the dal. Avni, you did okay today.

qa.a: The Saturday photography course.

qa.a: Avni felt relieved and moved, nearly crying into the dal after bracing for a fight.

passage: In Sirsa, Jatin had farmed the family's cotton fields since he was eighteen, because his father's knees gave out and because nobody had ever asked him anything else. This winter, reading at night by the tube light, he realised he had never once decided to be a farmer. He had just stepped into Bapu's boots. He didn't sell the land or run to the city, as his cousin had. Instead he kept the cotton, tried vegetables for the town market on one acre near the well, and signed up for a weekend agriculture course in Hisar. At dinner he explained to his mother, Aparna, 'I'm not leaving what Bapu built. I'm finding out which parts are mine.' She served him extra saag and said, 'Your Bapu wanted that too, once.'

Class 5 note, week before the Christmas break.
Sarika and Sunaina have been inseparable since June: same bench, matching hair clips, notes passed in a code only they understand. Today at the class party, Sunaina told a group that Sarika still sleeps with a stuffed elephant. The group laughed. Sarika went completely white, ran to the washroom, and I found her crying so hard she couldn't speak. She kept saying, 'I only told her. Only her.' I sat with her until she could breathe, then spoke with Sunaina separately. Sunaina said she hadn't meant it to be mean and began to cry too. Next step: on Monday I will offer them quiet time together to talk, with me nearby, and let Sarika decide if she wants that.

passage:
Dussehra holidays, Friday night.
Dear diary, Pema is my best friend. I've told him everything: that I'm scared of the dark, that I cried when our dog died, that I want to be a chef, not an engineer. He's the only one who knows the chef part. We promised to make the Ravana model together for the colony contest. Today I went to his house with the bamboo sticks, and he and Tsering were already building it. Pema said, 'Tsering's dad has a glue gun, sorry yaar.' Sorry yaar!! Like it's nothing. Lokesh

passage: Everyone in Class 10B thought Binita had it together: glossy notes, a hundred friends, a laugh you could hear across the Bhubaneswar school grounds. 'Nice post,' Dhruv said, sliding his phone across the canteen table. 'Five hundred likes for a sunset.'
'Five hundred and twelve,' Anirban said, grinning.
'You looked so happy in the pic.'
'I was.'
'You were panicking about the physics test five minutes before. I was there.'

'I might.'
Anirban stopped folding. 'I'm not sure about anything right now. Marks, college, what I'm even good at.' He looked up fast. 'Don't make it a thing.'
'Not a thing,' Dhruv said. 'Eat your samosa. Then tell me more.'

passage: I'm Sarita, and for the first four months with Mehak I kept a door half-closed. We met in the college theatre club, and I liked her more than I'd ever liked anyone. She thought I didn't care. One night she said, 'I feel like I'm dating a very polite stranger.' That line stayed with me. Slowly, I tried: one real thing a week. The first was tiny, that I hate my own laugh. Later, bigger things. I still keep my own friends and my Sunday runs; I'm not disappearing into her. passage:

passage:
Sunday night.
Eight hundred contacts in my phone, three group chats pinging all day, and I spent Saturday night eating alone in front of reruns. That's when I decided. No more hundred shallow hellos. I'm picking a few. Today I called Shalini, the first time in months that wasn't a birthday message. We fought last year about her wedding; I said something stupid about her fiance, and we never fixed it. So I started with that. 'I was wrong, and I've missed you.' It was so awkward. Long silence. Then she said, 'I missed you too, you idiot.' We talked for two hours. I told her the truth, that the new job is lonely and I'm struggling. She didn't fix it; she just listened. We're doing Sundays now. Jomon, one real friend beats a hundred group chats.

qa.q: How many contacts does Jomon have?
qa.a: Eight hundred contacts.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel during the long silence on the call?
qa.a: Jomon felt awkward and nervous, unsure whether Shalini would accept the apology.

qa.q: What makes Jomon's approach likely to ease the loneliness?
qa.a: Investing in a few people, repairing the old fight honestly and sharing real struggles builds closeness that numbers can't.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt hearing the apology?
qa.a: Shalini was probably moved and relieved, since she had missed Jomon too, as her teasing 'you idiot' shows.

grounding: A lonely young adult with many contacts chooses depth: an awkward repair, an honest admission and a regular call.

passage: In the kasba of Bhadrak, everyone knew Varun. He ran the photocopy shop by the bus stand, nodded to fifty people a day and was invited to every wedding. He asked Nazia, his old school friend who now taught at the girls' school, to have tea every Thursday at the stall by the tank. The first Thursday was awkward; they had drifted after she moved away. He told her, stumbling, that he felt lonely here, which he had never said aloud. She admitted she did too. On the third Thursday they argued about a film and she walked off annoyed. On the fourth he brought her favourite jalebi and said sorry. She laughed. They're still doing Thursdays.

passage: At the primary health centre in Kottur, Lakshmi had worked beside Pema for three months, and she still knew almost nothing about him. He came from Darjeeling; that was all. When the others asked about family, he smiled and turned the talk to blood-test reports. He skipped the staff Onam lunch. Lakshmi didn't push. Each evening, walking to the bus stop past the paddy fields, she simply called, 'Walking. Come if you like.' For two weeks he said he had work. Then one day he fell into step beside her without a word. They walked in silence to the bus stop. The next week he mentioned his mother's momos. A month later, on the same road, he told her quietly that nobody had visited him since he moved. Lakshmi just listened, and kept walking.

passage: In the London accounts office, Tariq noticed that Kofi always ate lunch at his desk, headphones on, and answered 'Fine, thanks' to every question about his weekend. qa.a: They were short and simple, a ten-minute coffee walk, and he accepted each no without fuss and didn't fill the silences.

qa.a: It suggests Kofi is beginning to trust Tariq and wants the company, even if he says it lightly.

grounding: An office worker abroad notices a withdrawn colleague and keeps offering short coffee walks, letting trust build at his pace.

passage: Deepak, you asked why I keep a diary at seventy. Let me tell you about when I was fifteen, in Rajkot. Two old aunts lived with us. Motiba laughed at everything, fed every stray cat and told stories of her girlhood as if they happened yesterday. Kaki sat by the window counting what people had done to her, fifty years of grudges, each one polished like brass. I used to sit between them and think, 'Hansa, which one will you be?' I didn't understand then that it isn't decided at seventy. It's decided in small choices, every year. But that question never left me. It's why I write down one good thing every night. Kaki taught me that as much as Motiba did.

qa.a: In Rajkot.

qa.a: It stayed and later became the habit of writing one good thing every night, a small daily choice towards contentment.

qa.a: Kaki likely felt bitter and wronged, holding on to old hurts that kept her from enjoying the present.

passage: The power went out at the old-age home in Madurai just as Karthik and his sister Irawati arrived with their grandfather's lunch. For two hours, in the heat, with the fans dead, they waited in the common room. Thatha grumbled the whole time: the food was cold, his sons were ungrateful, the world had gone to the dogs. Across the room, Mrs Fernandes, older and in a wheelchair, started a sing-along by candlelight and laughed when she forgot the words. 'How is she so happy?' Karthik whispered. 'She has less than Thatha.' Irawati fanned herself with a newspaper. 'Maybe she decided to be.' Karthik watched the candle flicker and felt a strange chill in the heat. Could you decide? When? He didn't know, but he kept looking from one to the other until the lights came back.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes start during the power cut?
qa.a: A sing-along by candlelight.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he watched the candle flicker?
qa.a: Karthik felt puzzled and a little unsettled, wondering whether contentment in old age is decided, and when.

qa.q: What could Karthik do with the question the visit raised?
qa.a: He could talk with Mrs Fernandes and Thatha about their lives, and notice which of his own habits lean towards gratitude or grudges.

qa.a: Thatha seems bitter and resentful, probably also lonely, feeling his sons are ungrateful and the world has gone wrong.

grounding: During a power cut a teenage boy compares his bitter grandfather with a cheerful resident and wonders how old age is shaped.

passage:
Tuesday, 1 am.
Couldn't sleep. After the career talk today I imagined myself at sixty: a bank job I never questioned, a nice flat, and Amma gone without my ever saying sorry for the years I barely spoke to her after Appa left. The picture made my throat close. For an hour I did the old thing: made a ten-year plan, perfect grades, perfect internships, perfect everything, so I'd never regret anything. Then I tore it up, because that's just a different way of wasting a life. Jyoti said something at lunch: 'You can't plan your way out of regret. You can only do the next honest thing.' So here's mine. Tomorrow I'll call Amma, not to be perfect, just to say I'm sorry and I miss her.
Rukmini, go to sleep.

qa.q: What did Jyoti say at lunch?
qa.a: 'You can't plan your way out of regret. You can only do the next honest thing.'

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when picturing life at sixty?
qa.a: Rukmini felt a frightened, regretful ache, the throat closing at the thought of never apologising to Amma.

qa.q: Why is calling Amma a better answer to the fear than the ten-year plan?
qa.a: It acts honestly on the regret now, while the perfect plan would only trade one kind of wasted life for another.

qa.q: How might Amma feel receiving that call?
qa.a: Amma would likely feel surprised and deeply moved, hearing her child say sorry and miss her after years of distance.

grounding: A student's diary imagines a regretful old age, slides towards perfectionism, then chooses one honest act now.

passage: At the farewell for old Negi-ji at the Kalpa post office, the retiring postmaster said something that stuck to Tenzin like a burr: 'Forty years sorting other people's letters, and I never once wrote the ones I wanted to.' He was twenty, packing apples for his uncle, never asked what he wanted, never having told his mother he had forgiven her for sending him to boarding school. What if he was Negi-ji at sixty? 'Stop planning a perfect life,' she said. 'Just write one letter.' He wrote to his mother that morning. Then he asked the forest office about their guide training.
